packet.headline_seed: Father leaves 7-year-old son alone on Mount Fuji to continue hike, reports say
packet.description_seed: The man had taken his two boys on the trip but is said to have left one behind when he got tired.

what: Father leaves 7-year-old son alone on Mount Fuji to continue hike, reports say

clean_source_blocks.text: According to reports, the boy was found on his own at 07:30 local time on Thursday (22:30 GMT). Officers castigated his father when he returned from the higher station and reunited with his son, who is said to have been "tired and fussy" after eight hours of waiting. "Even if it means having to give up on climbing the mountain together, leaving a child behind is unacceptable," one told him, according to Japan Today. He is said to have apologised for the "rash" decision. The family was reported to have been on the Fujinomiya route, which starts from the fifth station on the mountain, a spot which is accessible by public transport. From there it takes around five hours to reach the peak and a further three hours to get down, climbing guides suggest.

A man who left his seven-year-old son on Mount Fuji alone while he hiked has been reprimanded by police. The boy was taken into police custody after he was found sitting on a bench 6,600ft up Japan's highest mountain in fog and rain with only a soft drink and a snack on Thursday morning. The boy, from Nagoya, said he had started climbing the hill with his 48-year-old father and his brother, but had complained of being too tired to continue. His father had told him to "wait here", SBS TV reported, while he continued the 12,389ft ascent with his elder son, who had gone on ahead. TV Asahi said the boy had been told to wait for hours at the sixth station of the mountain, with no money.

Depicted by Japanese artists including Hokusai, Mt Fuji's distinctive, snow-capped cone is a national icon - Itsuo Inouye/AP Staff at a mountain hut alerted police to his presence after spotting him on his own at 7.30am local time (10.30pm UK time). They invited the boy inside the hut and let him take shelter there while they waited for officers to arrive. Officers contacted the father, who had reached the eighth station, and handed the boy over to him when he arrived. It was estimated that the boy had been left for around three hours, Japan Today reported. The police officer told AFP that officers gave the man a scolding for leaving the child behind. original_article.research:
[Lähde: BBC World | URL: https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c93403wg288o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss]
The boy was found alone on Japan's highest mountain

A father has been reprimanded by police after leaving his son on Japan's highest mountain for several hours with just a soft drink and snack, local media report.

The seven-year-old was spotted sitting on a bench on Mount Fuji in foggy and rainy conditions, at a point situated at over 2,000m (6,500ft).

His father, 48, reportedly told him to "wait here" after the boy complained he was tired - and continued the climb with his elder son.

Staff at a mountain hut found the child near the sixth station of a hiking route towards the summit and alerted police. His father was tracked down at the route's eighth station - said to be a three-hour hike away.

According to reports, the boy was found on his own at 07:30 local time on Thursday (22:30 GMT).

Officers castigated his father when he returned from the higher station and reunited with his son, who is said to have been "tired and fussy" after eight hours of waiting.

"Even if it means having to give up on climbing the mountain together, leaving a child behind is unacceptable," one told him, according to Japan Today. He is said to have apologised for the "rash" decision.

The family was reported to have been on the Fujinomiya route, which starts from the fifth station on the mountain, a spot which is accessible by public transport.

From there it takes around five hours to reach the peak and a further three hours to get down, climbing guides suggest.

Mount Fuji climber rescued twice after going back for lost phone

Mount Fuji, which stands at a height of 3,776m (12,389ft), has been the site of a number of climbing mishaps in recent years.

In July, a 99-year-old woman had to be rescued attempting the route after falling and hurting her hip and back.

And last year, a 27-year-old university student who went outside of official climbing season had to be rescued twice in four days - after he went back to look for his lost mobile phone.

Mount Fuji, an active volcano located south-west of Tokyo, was granted World Heritage status in 2013.

It is also one of three traditional "Holy Mountains" together with Mount Tate and Mount Haku.

Around 200,000 people climb it each year, but there are daily caps on some routes to avoid overcrowding.
